intro_blocks.text: Four resources are required for a camp to become a permanent settlement:

Oxygen provides breathable air for the crew and propellant for the vehicles. Water sustains life and, when split by electricity, provides fuel. Energy, both solar and nuclear fission, is the currency that pays for extracting the first two. Access to Earth allows the transport of crew and cargo, the lifeline the other three are slowly working to make optional.

features.label: F_01 — Site
features.title: de Gerlache Crater Rim Outpost
features.text: The outpost sits directly on the crater rim. The crest holds near-continuous sunlight for power, and a few hundred meters away, a small cold trap offers permanently shadowed ground for the first water-harvesting tests. Farther out, in rover range, the floor of de Gerlache itself: a vast darkness unbroken for roughly two billion years, where the large ice deposits are believed to wait.

features.label: F_02 — Landing Zone 1
features.title: The Landing Pad — ISRU Experiment
features.text: This pad is built from the moon ground itself by the base's own ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization) machinery. An excavator grades the site, then focused solar heat sinters the regolith at around 1,100 °C, fusing loose dust into a hard ceramic surface with no water, no cement, and no imports. The result is the port's protective architecture, a solid pad that kills the dust a landing would otherwise throw at bullet-like speeds, ringed by a berm to catch what the engines kick loose. On it stands Blue Origin's Mk2, the base's routine ride for crew and cargo.

features.label: F_03 — Landing Zone 2
features.title: Heavy Cargo
features.text: SpaceX's Starship HLS (Human Landing System) delivers up to 100 tonnes in a single landing, entirely changing the math of building a lunar outpost. It stands two kilometers from the base on open ground, where distance itself is the safety buffer. Cargo rides an elevator down the hull from a bay about 30 meters up, making the tallest structure on the Moon also its freight terminal.

features.label: F_04 — Operations Hub
features.title: Habitat, Power, and Research
features.text: The habitat cluster rises at the center of the base, its vertical solar wings tracking a sun that never climbs. Daylight power is solar, while night and contingency power come from a fission unit parked a kilometer up-slope, close enough to cable, far enough to fail safely. Around the habitat, the base's working machinery spreads across the crest: the water-harvesting experiment at a nearby cold trap, and the plant that extracts oxygen from the lunar regolith.

blocks.text: Building a Moon Base That Doesn't Exist Yet

I have tried looking for a picture or a video of what a real lunar base would actually look like, but I haven't found one. There are artist impressions, and there are NASA documents, but the impressions ignore the engineering, and the documents have no pictures worth staring at. Nothing lets you stand on the actual ground, under the actual light, next to hardware that follows the actual published designs. So I decided to build it myself: a Moon base you can look around in your browser, where every structure traces to a real design and every shadow is computed, not painted. This page is the result, and this article explains how it was made.

The terrain under this base is not sculpted by hand. It uses real Moon DEM (Digital Elevation Model) data from NASA. I started from NASA's laser altimetry of the lunar South Pole, at five meters per pixel, and kept it at true scale. Then I let the data choose the site, with the help of Claude Code and a Blender MCP connection. Hundreds of candidate positions were scored on slope, sunlight, and distance to shadowed ice, and the analysis produced a discovery that shaped everything that followed: the flattest ground typically lay in basins that a full lighting simulation proved dark at every sun angle. On polar terrain, the easy ground and the lit ground are almost never the same ground. From a short list of viable candidates, I hand-picked the rim of de Gerlache Crater.

blocks.caption: Map of the Moon's South Pole with the de Gerlache crater rim highlighted.

blocks.text: Lunar polar light is unique, and I didn't want to fake it. The sun here never rises. It circles, never climbing more than a hand's width above the horizon, dragging kilometer-long shadows around the base like the hand of a slow clock. I lit the scene using the correct solar intensity and geometry. The only compromise I made was adding a little ambient light to the shadowed areas, standing in for the faint real-world scatter from sunlit slopes, so you can still identify some terrain features hidden inside them.

blocks.caption: The de Gerlache Crater. Animation of the monthly sunlight rotation.

blocks.text: From Path Tracing to Interactive Web Experience

The biggest technical challenge for me was making cinematic, interactive lighting run smoothly in a web browser on both laptops and phones. With typical ray-tracing techniques, cinematic light cannot be computed efficiently on a phone at high frame rates. Additionally, file sizes become far too large when using high-poly models and high-resolution textures. Gaussian splatting turned out to be the perfect solution for both bottlenecks. The scene is path-traced in Blender's Cycles at full physical accuracy, then captured into 3D Gaussian splats, a technique that bakes the finished light into millions of tiny volumetric points a browser can render in real time.

blocks.caption: From data to scene. elevation model, clay render, final light, capture rig.

blocks.text: The scene is set in 2032, following the schedule NASA had sketched at the time this project was created. Of course, mission schedules and plans tend to evolve over time. Depending on audience interest, I might update this scene as those plans change. I also have ideas for introducing other space engineering concepts like this one. If I focus my time on building entirely new concepts, this specific Moon base page might not receive frequent updates. Let me know what you find more interesting: exploring brand new concepts, or keeping this base updated as NASA's real plans evolve. You can leave your email below to get notified when something new goes live.
Thank you for your time and your interest in this project.
